source_evidence.anchor: opening setup before Algorithm 1 and equation (1)
source_evidence.observation: The standing setup takes A in R^{m x n}, with m >= n and rank(A) = n. It writes A by columns and describes exact-arithmetic QR with Q^T Q = I_n and nonsingular upper-triangular R.

Algorithm 2 initializes r_11 = ||a_1||_2 and, for k = 2,...,n, computes s_k = Q_{k-1}^T a_k, v_k = a_k - Q_{k-1}s_k, psi_k = ||a_k||_2, phi_k = ||s_k||_2, r_kk = (psi_k-phi_k)^{1/2}(psi_k+phi_k)^{1/2}, and q_k = v_k/r_kk.

The paper assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic, gives fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), |delta| <= epsilon_M, for normalized-range results, and adopts a first-order linearization that discards O(epsilon_M^2) contributions.

The paper defines c_1(m,1)=1, c_1(m,k)=2 sqrt(2mk)+2 sqrt(k) for k>=2; c_2(m,1)=m+2, c_2(m,k)=3.5mk^2-1.5mk+16k for k>=2; c_3=0.5c_2; c_4=c_2+2c_1; A_k as the first k columns of A; and kappa_2(R_k)=||R_k||_2||R_k^{-1}||_2.

For the R produced by Algorithm 2, Theorem 1 assumes c_4(m,k) epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 for every prefix and concludes, for k=1,...,n and to within O(epsilon_M^2), that ||I-Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k) kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M.

The enclosing theorem also defines Delta A_k = Q_kR_k-A_k and E_k=R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k, bounds them by c_1(m,k)||A_k||_2 epsilon_M and c_2(m,k)||A_k||_2^2 epsilon_M, compares ||R_k||_2 with ||A_k||_2 through c_3, and bounds ||Q_k||_2 by sqrt(2).

source_evidence.anchor: paragraph immediately following Theorem 1 and opening of Remark 1
source_evidence.observation: The paper states that condition (3) assures nonsingularity and the validity of (7) and (8), and emphasizes that the stated condition and orthogonality bound use kappa_2(R_k), not kappa_2(A_k).
When the assumptions of Theorem 1 fail, phi_k can be at least psi_k, causing Algorithm 2 to break down and produce nonreal Q and R.
Using condition (3), the proof treats R as nonsingular, obtains r_kk > 0, and concludes that the computed quantities must satisfy psi_k > phi_k.

source_evidence.anchor: Appendix proof, exact identity following 'To get (7)'
source_evidence.observation: From Q_k=(A_k+Delta A_k)R_k^{-1}, the proof gives an exact identity expressing I-Q_k^TQ_k as R_k^{-T} times E_k-A_k^T Delta A_k-(Delta A_k)^T A_k-(Delta A_k)^T Delta A_k times R_k^{-1}.

source_evidence.anchor: Appendix proof, norm estimate following the exact identity
source_evidence.observation: Taking spectral norms and applying the bounds for E_k and Delta A_k yields c_4(m,k)||R_k||_2^2||R_k^{-1}||_2^2 epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2), where c_4=c_2+2c_1.

binders: Standing input: dimensions m,n with m >= n and a real matrix A in R^{m x n} having rank(A)=n. This is stated before the algorithms and inherited by Theorem 1 rather than repeated in the theorem heading. [PDF p. 2 (printed 300), anchor: opening setup before equation (1)]
Prefix index: k ranges over 1,...,n; A_k is the matrix formed from the first k columns of A. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: definitions (2) and Theorem 1]

Computed objects: Q_k in R^{m x k} and upper-triangular R_k in R^{k x k} are the k-column prefixes constructed by floating-point Algorithm 2; these dimensions are inherited from its block construction. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1]
Floating-point parameter: epsilon_M is the machine unit of the assumed arithmetic. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: floating-point model following Algorithm 2]
hypotheses: The output must be produced by Algorithm 2, the Cholesky-like or pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt variant CGS-P. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1]
For every k=1,...,n, the strict smallness condition c_4(m,k) epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 is required. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3)]
The standing matrix setup assumes m >= n and rank(A)=n. [PDF p. 2 (printed 300), anchor: opening setup before equation (1)]

The analysis uses IEEE floating-point arithmetic for normalized-range results and deliberately neglects second- and higher-order roundoff terms. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: floating-point model and linear approximation]
conclusions: Selected theorem conclusion: for every k=1,...,n, ||I_k-Q_k^TQ_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k) kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M, understood to within terms of O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1, inequality (7) and its preamble]

Supporting exact proof identity: I_k-Q_k^TQ_k = R_k^{-T}(E_k-A_k^T Delta A_k-(Delta A_k)^T A_k-(Delta A_k)^T Delta A_k)R_k^{-1}. [PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: Appendix proof, exact identity deriving (7)]

Supporting norm estimate: ||I_k-Q_k^TQ_k||_2 <= ||R_k^{-1}||_2^2(||E_k||_2+2||Delta A_k||_2||A_k||_2+||Delta A_k||_2^2), which becomes c_4(m,k)||R_k||_2^2||R_k^{-1}||_2^2 epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: Appendix proof, norm estimate deriving (7)]
definitions_and_conventions: A=(a_1,...,a_n), Q=(q_1,...,q_n), and R=(r_jk); A_k, Q_k, and R_k denote the corresponding first-k-column or leading-prefix objects. [PDF p. 2 (printed 300), anchor: notational conventions; PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: Algorithm 2]
Delta A_k is the factorization residual defined exactly by Delta A_k=Q_kR_k-A_k. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1, equation (4)]
E_k is the normal-equation residual defined exactly by E_k=R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1, equation (5)]

The enclosing theorem supplies ||Delta A_k||_2 <= c_1(m,k)||A_k||_2 epsilon_M and ||E_k||_2 <= c_2(m,k)||A_k||_2^2 epsilon_M, within O(epsilon_M^2); these are inputs to the proof of (7). [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: equations (4)-(5); PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: proof of (7)]

I in inequality (7) is dimensionally I_k because Q_k^TQ_k is k x k; the theorem prints I without a subscript. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: inequality (7); PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: construction of Q_k]

Left orthogonality means Q^TQ=I; inequality (7) measures the failure of the computed Q_k to have this exact property. [PDF p. 2 (printed 300), anchor: explanation following equation (1); PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: inequality (7)]
implicit_context: The full-column-rank assumption is standing context from the paper's algorithm setup, not an explicitly repeated binder in Theorem 1. [PDF p. 2 (printed 300), anchor: opening setup; PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1]

Q_k and R_k are computed floating-point matrices subsequently interpreted as real matrices when transposes, inverses, products, and norms are taken in the analysis. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: Algorithm 2 and floating-point model; PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: exact identity deriving (7)]

Condition (3) is used to ensure that the required R_k inverses exist and that the orthogonality bound holds. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: paragraph following Theorem 1; PDF p. 9 (printed 307), anchor: Lemma 2 proof]

The enclosing multi-part theorem also states the factorization-residual bound (4), normal-equation-residual bound (5), norm comparison (6), and ||Q_k||_2 <= sqrt(2) in (8); the locator-selected claim is specifically (7), whose proof uses (4)-(6). [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1, equations (4)-(8); PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: proof of (6)-(8)]
statement.algorithm_linkage: The claim is tied specifically to CGS-P (Algorithm 2): r_11=||a_1||_2; for k>=2 it computes s_k=Q_{k-1}^Ta_k, v_k=a_k-Q_{k-1}s_k, psi_k=||a_k||_2, phi_k=||s_k||_2, and r_kk=(psi_k-phi_k)^{1/2}(psi_k+phi_k)^{1/2}, followed by q_k=v_k/r_kk. It is not a claim about standard CGS-S, which instead sets r_kk=||v_k||_2. [PDF p. 2 (printed 300), anchor: Algorithm 1 and comparison with Algorithm 2; PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: Algorithm 2]
numerical_model: The paper explicitly assumes floating-point arithmetic satisfying the IEEE standard. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: floating-point model following Algorithm 2]
The displayed local model is fl(x+y)=(x+y)(1+delta), with |delta|<=epsilon_M, for results in the normalized range. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: floating-point model following Algorithm 2]

For a modest function p(n), the analysis uses (1+epsilon_M)^{p(n)}=1+p(n)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) and assumes the O(epsilon_M^2) contribution is insignificant. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: linear approximation]

The proof applies standard floating-point error bounds to norms, inner products, matrix-vector products, subtraction, division, and square roots, but the selected passage does not provide a complete primitive-operation semantics for each of them. [PDF p. 9 (printed 307), anchor: Lemma 2 proof; PDF pp. 10-11 (printed 308-309), anchor: proof equations (16)-(20)]
error_notions: The selected error is absolute loss of column orthogonality, measured by ||I_k-Q_k^TQ_k||_2; it is not an error relative to a separately specified exact Q. [PDF p. 2 (printed 300), anchor: definition of left orthogonality; PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: inequality (7)]

The derivation decomposes orthogonality loss into the normal-equation residual E_k and the factorization residual Delta A_k, including both linear cross terms and the quadratic term (Delta A_k)^T Delta A_k. [PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: exact identity deriving (7)]

The residual bounds used are normwise rather than componentwise: ||Delta A_k||_2 is proportional to ||A_k||_2 and ||E_k||_2 is proportional to ||A_k||_2^2. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: equations (4)-(5)]
norms: All norms in the selected theorem bound are 2-norms. For matrices this is the spectral/operator 2-norm, as also indicated by ||R_k||_2^2=||R_k^TR_k||_2 in the proof. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: definitions and inequality (7); PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: proof of (6)]
kappa_2(R_k) is defined as ||R_k||_2||R_k^{-1}||_2, using an ordinary inverse rather than a pseudoinverse. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: definition preceding Theorem 1]
The condition number appears squared in both hypothesis (3) and conclusion (7). [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: conditions (3) and (7)]

The theorem's literal bound is expressed through the computed R_k condition number, not kappa_2(A_k); Remark 1 discusses only a modified restatement in terms of A_k. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: opening of Remark 1]
constants_and_indexing: For k=1, c_1(m,1)=1 and c_2(m,1)=m+2. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: definitions (2)]
For k=2,...,n, c_1(m,k)=2 sqrt(2mk)+2 sqrt(k). [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: definitions (2)]
For k=2,...,n, c_2(m,k)=3.5mk^2-1.5mk+16k. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: definitions (2)]
For every relevant k, c_3(m,k)=0.5c_2(m,k) and c_4(m,k)=c_2(m,k)+2c_1(m,k). [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: definitions (2)]

Both the hypothesis and conclusion apply prefix-by-prefix for k=1,...,n; Algorithm 2 handles k=1 by initialization and k>=2 by its loop. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1]
The smallness condition is strict: c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 must be less than 1, not less than or equal to 1. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: condition (3)]
higher_order_terms: Theorem 1 qualifies all displayed conclusions as valid to within terms of O(epsilon_M^2), even though inequality (7) itself prints no remainder term. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: Theorem 1 preamble and inequality (7)]
The appendix's derived form explicitly ends with c_4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: final norm estimate deriving (7)]

The quadratic residual term contributes at second order because ||Delta A_k||_2=O(epsilon_M); it is retained in the exact identity and absorbed into O(epsilon_M^2) in the final bound. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: equation (4); PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: exact identity and norm estimate]

No explicit coefficient, sign, threshold, or uniformity statement is supplied for the O(epsilon_M^2) remainder. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: linear approximation; PDF p. 14 (printed 312), anchor: final estimate]
exceptional_values: The relative-error model is stated only for results in the normalized range, so the cited model does not cover overflow, underflow into subnormals, infinities, or NaNs. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: floating-point model following Algorithm 2]
Without Theorem 1's assumptions, phi_k>=psi_k can make the square-root expression for r_kk nonreal and cause Algorithm 2 to break down. [PDF p. 7 (printed 305), anchor: Remark 2]

Under condition (3), the proof treats every needed R_k as nonsingular, obtains r_kk>0, and hence requires psi_k>phi_k. [PDF p. 4 (printed 302), anchor: paragraph following Theorem 1; PDF p. 9 (printed 307), anchor: Lemma 2 proof]
The passage gives no separate assumptions about input representability, signed zero, NaNs, infinities, or a specific IEEE rounding mode. [PDF p. 3 (printed 301), anchor: stated floating-point model]

contract_plain_english: For a real full-column-rank A with m>=n, run the pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt Algorithm 2 in the paper's IEEE-style, normalized-range, first-order floating-point model. If every computed leading triangular factor R_k satisfies the strict condition c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2<1, then every computed Q_k has spectral-norm loss of orthogonality at most c_4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2epsilon_M to first order, with an unspecified O(epsilon_M^2) remainder. The proof obtains this by an exact decomposition through the factorization residual Delta A_k and normal-equation residual E_k. The claim uses the computed R_k condition number, including its square, and depends specifically on Algorithm 2's pythagorean diagonal calculation.
